title: Packetized probe-and-warmstart kernel strategy for bimodal sequence-length workloads
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Background: Several Redwood customers exhibit bimodal sequence length distributions (short chat turns ~20-40 tokens and long context summarizations ~1500+ tokens) that cause our current kernel selection heuristics to oscillate between prefill-optimized and decode-optimized kernels, leading to latency spikes and reduced throughput under mixed load.

Goal: Implement a packetized probe-and-warmstart strategy that (1) quickly probes a small representative subset of requests to infer per-request preferred kernel paths (arch + seqlen bucket + quantization profile), (2) caches warmstart decisions keyed by a lightweight fingerprint, and (3) schedules prefill/decode so that short-turn requests are not delayed by transient kernel reconfiguration. The feature should reduce 95th-percentile latency for mixed loads and improve overall throughput without regressing single-mode workloads.

High-level approach:
- Add a fast, non-blocking probe stage at request admission: run microbenchmarks (microprobe) on a tiny token window or a synthetic short decode to sample latency/cost across 2-3 candidate kernels using a budgeted selector (<= 1% added compute).
- Generate a compact fingerprint combining model variant, device family, truncated seqlen histogram (prefill vs decode hints), and request metadata. Store warmstart mapping in an LRU cache with TTL and eviction hints based on observed drift.
- Introduce packetized scheduling that groups short-turn requests into an express path pinned to warmstart kernels, while long-context prefill requests are batched differently to avoid kernel churn.
- Integrate with existing kernel-cost models and add an online feedback loop: use observed per-token latency and memory pressure to update kernel preference scores and invalidate warmstarts when cost delta exceeds threshold.

Why different from previous autotuners: This solution focuses on live, per-request microprobes and warmstarts rather than offline profiling or global bandit policies. It targets mixed, bimodal traffic where quick per-request decisions prevent tail latency amplification.

Risks and mitigations:
- Probe overhead: cap probing to a small percentage of requests and short microbench lengths; run probes opportunistically during CPU idle windows.
- Cache staleness after model/quantization updates: invalidate cache on rollout events and version bump.
- Increased scheduler complexity: keep express path conservative and add feature flag rollout with telemetry gating.

acceptance_criteria: Canary at 1% traffic shows no more than 3% regression in median latency and no increase in error rate
95th-percentile latency improvement of at least 15% on mixed bimodal synthetic workload compared to baseline
Warmstart cache hit rate >= 70% after steady-state within 30 minutes under representative traffic
Feature gated behind runtime flag with Console toggle and audit log entries on enable/disable
Automated tests covering probe lifecycle, cache TTL and invalidation on model rollouts
notes: Experiment plan: use mixed workload generator (20% long-context, 80% short turns) with variable QPS to measure tail latency and throughput
Metrics to track: median/95/99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization, kernel switch frequency, warmstart hit/miss ratio, per-request probe count, tail memory pressure events
Fallback policy: if probe fails or returns ambiguous results, fall back to conservative default kernel for the model family
Rollout plan: dev -> internal services -> canary 1% -> canary 5% -> gradual ramp 25% -> all routes (conditional on metrics)
